                                 Tilo Arens
                      (joint work with Armin Lechleiter)

In an inverse scattering problem, the aim is to obtain a reconstruction of a scatterer
or value of a refractive index from the knowledge of the far field pattern of the
scattered wave for one or several known incident fields. For the purpose of this talk,
we consider the simplest type of a scattering problem, where a scalar (i.e. acoustic)
field ui is incident on a bounded obstacle D ⊂ R3 . The total field is assumed to
vanish on the boundary of D.

   Sullivan and Morgan [26, 19] showed that the fundamental group of a formal
space is a 1-formal group. There exist non-formal spaces with 1-formal fundamental
groups, but Sullivan and Morgan’s theorem does have a partial converse. Papadima
and Suciu [20] proved that for a connected, finite-type CW complex X, if H ∗ (X, Q)
is a Koszul algebra and π1 (X) is a 1-formal group, then X is a formal space.
   In [4], Berceanu and Papadima prove certain motion groups, denoted P Σn , are
1-formal groups. The groups P Σn have a long history. David Dahm, in his unpub-
lished PhD thesis [11], considered arrangements of n unknotted, unlinked circles in
3-space and the corresponding group P Σn of motions of the arrangement in which
each circle ends at its original position. In [14], Goldsmith explained Dahm’s work
and realized P Σn as a subgroup of the automorphism group of the free group of
rank n; she also determined specific generators of P Σn .
   In [18], McCool found a presentation of P Σn in terms of relations of the gener-
ators found by Goldsmith. In the paper [6], Brownstein and Lee were interested
in the representation theory of P Σn and successfully computed the second integral
cohomology H 2 (P Σn , Z); they also conjectured a presentation for the entire coho-
mology algebra H ∗ (P Σn , Z). Over ten years later, Jensen, McCammond and Meier
in [15] proved the conjecture of Brownstein and Lee. In particular, they showed
H ∗ (P Σn , Q) is a quadratic algebra, a necessary condition for Koszulity.
   Berceanu and Papadima [4] also established 1-formality for the related group
P Σ+n called the upper triangular McCool group. Cohen and Pruidze [9] proved
H ∗ (P Σ+

Theorem 1.1. For n ≥ 4, the algebra H ∗ (P Σn , Q) is not Koszul.
   This raises the possibility that K(P Σn , 1) is not a formal space, but we do
not know if this is the case. Papadima and Yuzvinsky showed in [21] that for
X, a formal, connected, topological space with finite Betti numbers, the Koszul
property of H ∗ (X, Q) is equivalent to X being a rational K[π, 1] space, i.e., the Q-
completion of X is aspheric. The proof of Theorem 1.1 is given in Section 3. One
should contrast Theorem 1.1 with the fact that several families of algebras naturally
related to H ∗ (P Σn , Q) are Koszul. Besides H ∗ (P Σ+

Lemma 2.2. Let n, E, and I be as in Theorem 2.1. The quadratic algebra (E/I)!

Proof. If α∗ij denotes the graded dual of the generator αij , the mapping xij 7→ α∗ij on
the degree one generators is clearly surjective. There are n2 (n − 1)(n − 2)/2 linearly
independent relations listed, and the image of each vanishes on all relations of E/I

   The similarity to the relations of P Σn is not a coincidence. Lemma 2.2 shows
that (E/I)! is the universal enveloping algebra of a quadratic Lie algebra which we
denote by gn . The Lie algebra gn is the associated graded Lie algebra of the Mal’cev
Lie algebra of P Σn (see [4]). For more on the construction of gn , see Section 4.
Henceforth, we denote the quadratic dual algebra by U (gn ) rather than (E/I)! .
   As a consequence of Lemma 2.2, it is easy to see that U (g2 ) and U (g3 ) are Koszul
algebras; in fact, after a suitable change of variables, they are PBW-algebras in the
sense of Priddy [25].

Proposition 2.3. For n = 2 and n = 3, the algebras E/I and U (gn ) are isomorphic
to PBW-algebras. In particular, they are Koszul algebras.

Proof. The quadratic dual of a PBW-algebra is also a PBW-algebra, so it suffices
to show U (g2 ) and U (g3 ) are isomorphic to PBW algebras. The algebra U (g2 ) is a
free algebra on two generators, which is (trivially) a PBW-algebra. After making
the linear change of variables X1 = x21 + x31 , X2 = x12 + x32 , and X3 = x13 + x23 ,
the defining relations of U (g3 ) become

                    [x12 , X3 ], [x13 , X2 ], [x21 , X3 ],
                    [X3 − x13 , X1 ], [X1 − x21 , X2 ], [X2 − x12 , X1 ],
                    [x21 , X1 ], [x12 , X2 ], [x13 , X3 ]

Ordering monomials in the free algebra in deg-lex order where x12 > x13 > x21 >
X1 > X2 > X3 , there are no ambiguities among the high terms of the defining
relations. Therefore this alternate presentation of U (g3 ) has a quadratic Gröbner
basis. It follows that U (g3 ) is isomorphic to a PBW algebra, hence it is Koszul. 

   Thus the algebra U (g/h) is Koszul if and only if its Hilbert series is 1/(1 − 4t)2 .
Indeed, this was our motivation for considering the quotient U (g/h). The first nine
terms of the Maclaurin series of 1/(1 − 4t)2 are
 1 + 8t + 48t2 + 256t3 + 1280t4 + 6144t5 + 28672t6 + 131072t7 + 589824t8 + · · · .
As discussed in more detail below, we used the computer algebra system bergman
[1] (specifically the ncpbhgroebner method) to compute a Gröbner basis and the
Hilbert series for U (g/h) in degrees ≤ 8. We found the first 8 terms of the Hilbert
series to be
 1 + 8t + 48t2 + 256t3 + 1280t4 + 6144t5 + 28672t6 + 131072t7 + 589834t8 + · · · .
This computation demonstrates our result.
Theorem 3.6. The algebra U (g/h) is not Koszul. Consequently, U (gn ) is not
Koszul for n ≥ 4.
   We first performed this calculation several years ago using the 32-bit Windows
installation of bergman on an IBM ThinkPad T410 series with a 2.4 GHz Intel Core
i5 M520 processor and 3GB DDR3 RAM. The result has since been duplicated
several times on various systems and architectures as well as under GAP [13],
both by the authors and independently by Graham Denham, Frédéric Chapoton,
Bérénice Oger, and Jan-Erik Roos. We wish to thank them for their interest in
verifying Theorem 3.6.

    Our main tool is the recently developed graph limit method [6, 7, 4, 3] which is
